<strong>Karen Spärck Jones</strong> (193: Karen Spärck Jones (1935-2007) proposed the IDF weight in 1972, in a paper titled A Statistical Interpretation of Term Specificity and Its Application in Retrieval. She worked on information retrieval and language processing in Cambridge from the nineteen-fifties, when almost nobody thought computers had anything to do with words, and her formula is still inside search engines half a century later. A much quoted sentence is hers: “computing is too important to be left to men”.

Donde $N$ es el número de documentos y $:
Where $N$ is the number of documents and $n_t$ in how many of them the term $t$ appears.

If a word comes up in every document, $n_t = N$, the quotient is 1 and its weight is $\log 1 = 0$: it contributes nothing. If it comes up in just one out of a thousand, its weight is $\log 1000$, which is large. The logarithm is there so the thing does not run away.

With 27 sentences, “el” appears in 16 and its weight is $0{.}405$; “gato” is in 5 and weighs $1{.}686$; “queso” comes up in 1 and weighs $3{.}296$. Eight times more than the article.
El IDF de Spärck Jones formaliza esa ide: Spärck Jones's IDF formalises that idea: $\log(N/n_t)$ is zero for what is in every document.

And without likeness no generalisation is possible, because what is learned about cats cannot be carried over to anything.

Estos vectores son la base de casi toda: These vectors are the basis of almost all search by meaning. When a search engine finds a document that contains not one of the words you typed but talks about exactly that, what it has done is compare vectors, not words. The same is done by the systems that recommend similar articles, those that group news items about the same event and those that search a base of documents to hand it to a language model before it answers. The difference from what you have seen here is that those vectors do not come from counting neighbours but from training a network, but the geometry used afterwards — cosine, nearest neighbours — is exactly this one.
